Reading · the thing I was sure I couldn't do

1.1 Discuss. Is there a sport or an activity you have always wanted to try but never have? What has stopped you?

KEY WORDS

an opportunity a chance to do something

a beginner somebody doing it for the first time

to give it a go to try it

to put it off to keep delaying it

The Thing I Was Sure I Couldn't Do

We asked three readers about something they were afraid of, and did anyway.

SWIMMING, AT THIRTY-FOUR. I couldn't swim. Not badly — at all. I was terrified of deep water and I had put it off for twenty years, telling myself that if I were a child I would learn in a week, and that it was too late now. Then my daughter started lessons and asked me to come in with her. The first session was humiliating. The fourth was less humiliating. If somebody had told me at the start that I would swim a kilometre within a year, I would have laughed at them, and I would have been wrong.

THE FIRST RACE. I run alone, early, where nobody can see me, because I am not a proper runner and I am slightly ashamed of being slow. A friend signed us both up for a five-kilometre run without asking. I was furious with her. It turned out to be the least competitive event I have ever attended: there was no clock, somebody threw coloured powder at me every kilometre, and a man of about seventy passed me at four kilometres and said well done without any irony at all. If it had been a serious race I would never have finished. Because it wasn't, I did.

CLIMBING, AFRAID OF HEIGHTS. I am frightened of heights in the ordinary way: ladders, balconies, the third row of a stadium. A colleague was interested in bouldering — climbing without ropes, close to the ground — and needed somebody to go with. If you asked me now what the hardest part was, I would say the walk from the door to the wall, and nothing after it. Nobody looked at me. Everybody there was busy failing at their own problem, which turned out to be the entire point.

Three people, three things they were sure about. None of them was right.

2

Grammar · the second conditional

PRESENTATION

The second conditional is for things we imagine — situations that are not real now, and probably will not be.

form If + past simple, would + infinitive without to. If I was a bit fitter, I would definitely do it. · If you went, you would love it.

↔ Either half can come first. I'd do it if I was fitter. — no comma when the if half is second.

was/were was or were? Both are correct with I, he, she, it. If I were you… is slightly more formal; If I was you… is what most people say.

could could and might can replace would. If we went, we could get something to eat. · If I ever went to Thailand, I might try it.

The tense is not about time. If I went does not mean the past — it means this is imaginary. Compare the first conditional, which is about something genuinely possible: If it rains, we will stay in. · If it rained for a year, the whole city would float away.

First conditional — a real possibility

Second conditional — imagined

If I win, I'll buy a car.

If I won a million, I'd buy a house.

If she stays, she can help us.

If she stayed, she could help us.

If you don't drink coffee, you won't be awake.

If you didn't drink coffee, you wouldn't be awake.

(likely — it might really happen)

(unlikely, or untrue now)

ERROR WARNING

Three mistakes, and the first is by far the most common:

1 would in the if half. If I would see it again, I'd take a photo. ✗ → If I saw it again, I'd take a photo. ✓ would never follows if.

2 will in the result half. If you came with me, it will be fun. ✗ → If you came with me, it would be fun. ✓ One half imagined means both halves imagined.

3 can instead of could. If we went to the mall, we can get ice cream. ✗ → we could get ice cream ✓

A quick self-check. Put your finger over the if. If what is left says will or can, the sentence is a first conditional and the other half must be present. If it says would or could, the other half must be past.

PRONUNCIATION — WOULD ALMOST DISAPPEARS

In a positive sentence would is weak and contracted: I'd do it → /aɪdduːɪt/ · you'd love it → /juːdlʌvɪt/. You hear a d, not a word.

It is strong only when it carries the meaning: I WOULD like to, but… · Yes, I WOULD. And in the negative: I WOULDN'T do a full marathon.

So if you hear a stressed would, the speaker is contradicting something. That is worth knowing before you take it as enthusiasm.

Vocabulary · sport, and adjectives with prepositions

PRESENTATION — SPORT

Where you play: a court (tennis, basketball) · a pitch (football) · a track (running) · a net · a pool

Who is there: your opponent · a competitor · the referee · a coach · the spectators

What you do: train · compete · beat somebody · score a point · hit a shot · win or lose a match · take part in a race

Careful with beat and win. You beat a person or a team; you win a match, a race or a prize. We beat Italy ✓ · We won Italy ✗ · We won the match ✓

And sport is countable here: a sport for lazy people · three different sports. But do sport / play sport with no article is also common in British English.

PRESENTATION — ADJECTIVES + PREPOSITIONS

These pairs have to be learned together. There is no rule; there is only the pair.

of — afraid of · proud of · tired of · frightened of · full of

about — worried about · excited about · serious about · pleased about

in — interested in · involved in · with — popular with · furious with · bored with

for — essential for · famous for · responsible for · sorry for · to — similar to · married to · kind to

at — good at · bad at · surprised at

Careful: interested in, never interested about. · worried about, never worried for. · good at swimming, never good in swimming.

WHY YOU DIDN'T HEAR IT

would is a d. I'd be terrified → /aɪdbi/ · you'd love it → /juːdlʌvɪt/ · it'd be great → /ɪtədbi/ — that last one barely survives at all.

And the if half sounds past, so students translate it as past. If I went is not a memory; it is an imagined situation. Listen for the d in the other half — that is what tells you it is imaginary.

5

Everyday English · worries and reassurance

LISTENING INTO SPEAKING

Tom is going to ask Becky to marry him this evening. He has told one person: Mark, who proposed to Rachel a few years ago and is therefore the expert.

5.1 Listen to Parts 1 and 2, then answer.

1 What is Tom going to do, and how does he feel?

2 Where has he booked, and why did he choose it?

3 What two things is he worried about?

WORRIES AND REASSURANCE

Talking about a possible problem:

You don't think it's a bit boring? · I'm still worried that something will go wrong. · What if she says no?

Reassuring somebody:

You've got nothing to worry about. · I'm sure it'll be OK. · She's definitely not going to say no.

Notice the pattern. The worried person uses hedges — a bit, still, what if — and the reassuring person uses strong words — nothing, sure, definitely. Reassurance works by sounding more certain than you probably are.

5.2 Problem (P) or reassurance (R)?

1 You don't think it's a bit boring?

4 You've got nothing to worry about.

2 I'm sure it'll be OK.

5 What if she says no?

3 I'm still worried that something will go wrong.

6 She's definitely not going to say no.

5.3 Write a reassuring reply to each worry.

1 “What if nobody comes?” →

2 “I'm still worried that I'll forget my words.” →

3 “You don't think it's a bit too expensive?” →

PRONUNCIATION — SOUNDING SURE AND UNSURE

The same words can reassure or worry, depending on how you say them.

Sure: the voice is level or falling, the pace is steady, and there are no pauses. You've got nothing to worry about. ↘

Unsure: the voice rises at the end, the pace slows, and there are little pauses — Erm … fine, I think.

Why it matters here. Mark says I'm sure it'll be OK and sounds sure. When he talks about how worried he was, he sounds unsure — and that is the moment Tom stops believing him.

5.4 Sure (S) or unsure (U)? Then say each one both ways.

1 It'll be fine.

3 Yes, definitely.

2 It'll be … fine, I think.

4 Erm, yes, probably.

CHANGING THE SUBJECT

Conversations do not run in straight lines. Two phrases do almost all the steering:

That reminds me… — you are going somewhere new, and blaming the other person for it. That reminds me, I need to book the restaurant.

As I was saying… — you are going back to what you were talking about before you were interrupted. So, anyway, as I was saying, you've really changed my life.

One goes forward, one goes back, and in the model conversation they are used by two different people, one page apart. That is what a real conversation looks like.

5.5 Read the model, then answer.

MODEL

TOM So, erm, Becky — ever since I've known you…

BECKY It's been a long time since we were here last.

TOM Yeah, we came here on our first date, didn't we?

BECKY Really? I thought we went somewhere else. That reminds me — I need to book the restaurant for the office party. Let me just make a note before I forget. Were you trying to give me a ring earlier?

TOM A ring? What? No!

BECKY I've got a missed call from you on my phone.

TOM Oh — yeah, I just wanted to check you knew which restaurant it was. … So, anyway, as I was saying, you've really changed my life.

5.6 Answer about the model.

1 Who changes the subject, and who brings it back? Which phrase does each one use?

2 Becky says give me a ring. What does she mean, and what does Tom think she means?

3 Why is that misunderstanding funny at this exact moment?

4 Find three things Becky does that stop Tom finishing his sentence.

5.7 Work in pairs, then swap roles.

Student A — the worried one

Student B — the reassuring one

Choose one: a job interview tomorrow · a speech at a wedding · your first day teaching · asking somebody an important question.

Reassure A. Use all three reassuring phrases. Sound sure, even if you aren't.

Raise three worries, using a different phrase each time. Do not be reassured by the first answer.

At some point, change the subject with That reminds me… — and let A bring it back with As I was saying…

CHECK YOUR CONVERSATION

A used three different worry phrases — a bit, still worried that, what if. B used all three reassuring phrases.

B sounded sure — falling voice, no pauses, no erm. Somebody changed the subject and somebody brought it back.

A was not reassured by the first answer. (If A gives in immediately, there is nothing to practise.)
